clue.text: One prepared to gamble, unlike 22 on Friday

definitions.meaning: someone who stakes money on an outcome, a punter
in the nursery rhyme Solomon Grundy was 'worse on Friday', so he was the opposite of improved

explanation.surface: A gambler is contrasted with someone in a bad way at the end of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is Solomon Grundy, from the nursery rhyme: born on Monday, christened Tuesday, married Wednesday, took ill Thursday, worse Friday, died Saturday, buried Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: A punter is one who wagers, and the comparative of good is the opposite of worse, Grundy's state on Friday.

clue.text: Bird turning up any minute

indicators.note: in a down clue turning means the hidden letters are read upwards, backwards
up as in turning up, showing itself, says the bird is visible inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A bird is expected to show up at any moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft named no hidden-word signal; 'turning up' does both jobs in the surface, so 'up' (shows up) marks the hidden ANYM and 'turning' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: The myna is a starling-like Asian songbird known for mimicking speech.

clue.text: Plan to have study of substances for content of science

indicators.note: the inner letters, the contents, of the word science are swapped out for another piece

parts.note: taken as written
chemistry, abbreviated CHEM, is the study of substances

explanation.surface: Someone plans to study chemistry as part of a science course.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep the first and last letters S and E of 'science' and replace the inside CIENC with CHEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a systematic arrangement or design for doing something, a programme.

clue.text: Reason for a round-the-world race?

parts.note: not a sporting contest around the globe but a people, a race, found scattered round the world, and what put them there

explanation.surface: Someone asks what motivates a global yacht or car race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race' looks like a contest but means an ethnic people; the answer is the dispersal that spreads such a people worldwide.
explanation.definitionFit: A diaspora is the scattering of a people from their homeland across many countries.

clue.text: Totally elegant description of today's issue

definitions.text: Totally elegant description of today's issue

parts.words: Totally elegant description of today's issue
parts.note: the puzzle appeared on a Tuesday, so today's issue is not the newspaper but the baby born today, and the nursery rhyme line describing such a child says it is entirely graceful

explanation.surface: A reader praises the stylish design of today's newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' gives a line for each weekday's baby; the puzzle ran on a Tuesday. 'issue' means offspring, not an edition.
explanation.definitionFit: In the traditional rhyme the line for the second weekday's baby describes it as wholly elegant, matching the clue's praise.

clue.text: Hesitancy, mishandling events in state

indicators.note: handling something badly suggests the letters of the following words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Indecision leads to a botched response to events in a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mishandling' rearranges all thirteen letters of EVENTS IN STATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesitancy is uncertainty and caution, the quality of acting provisionally rather than decisively.

clue.text: Like Wednesday's new arrival — outside left — badly fouled

indicators.note: outside says the rearranged letters sit around the letter for left
badly signals the letters of the next word are messed up

explanation.surface: A footballer playing outside left is fouled badly, perhaps by a Wednesday side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' makes DOEFUL from FOULED, and 'outside' puts it around L. In the rhyme 'Wednesday's child is full of woe'; outside left is a football position.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby born on Wednesday, per the rhyme, is full of woe, which is to say mournful and sorrowful.

clue.text: Regular supply of 5 Across etc.

parts.note: babies like the second weekday's child, and those of every other day, keep arriving each day of the week, like a newspaper round

explanation.surface: Something like a newspaper or milk round brings a steady stream of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means a newspaper dropped off every morning; here it is births, one child for each day in the rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Births happen every day, so the children of the rhyme form a constant daily supply, a delivery in the obstetric sense.

clue.text: Measure of plane's speed for flier

definitions.meaning: aircraft and ships measure speed in nautical miles per hour
a wading bird of the sandpiper family, related to the dunlin

explanation.surface: Someone describes a pilot's speed reading for an aviator.
explanation.definitionFit: The nautical unit of one sea mile per hour gauges airspeed, and the same word names a shorebird that flies.

clue.text: Helpers aid reform in period of power

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Assistants help to bring about reforms while a government holds office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges the ten letters of HELPERS AID.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader's time in charge is called their tenure or command, so a spell in power fits.

clue.text: Just running, excellent, and beautiful, like first baby?

parts.note: fair means just or impartial
off means running or under way, as when a race is off
ace means excellent

explanation.surface: A list of qualities praises a baby: honest, energetic, superb and lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme begins 'Monday's child is fair of face', so the first baby of the week is the beautiful one.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the first weekday's child is good-looking, pretty in appearance.

clue.text: A seed that's the start of something big

parts.note: corn is grain, the seed of cereal plants

explanation.surface: A seed is praised as the origin of something large.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the proverb 'great oaks from little acorns grow'.
explanation.definitionFit: The oak's nut grows into a huge tree, so it is the beginning of a giant.

clue.text: Attached to labels identifying axes of stone

parts.note: on means attached to, as a label on a jar
Y and X are the letters that label the axes of a graph

explanation.surface: Tags are tied on to identify axes made of stone.
explanation.walkthrough: On a graph the horizontal and vertical axes are labelled X and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A banded variety of chalcedony used as a gemstone and in ornaments.

clue.text: See 5 Across
Grave occasions, such as 22's on Sunday

definitions.meaning: solemn events, with a pun on graves where the dead are buried
in the rhyme Solomon Grundy was 'buried on Sunday'

explanation.surface: Solemn events are compared to someone's Sunday activities.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is Solomon Grundy, whose rhyme ends 'buried on Sunday'.
explanation.definitionFit: Burial ceremonies are solemn affairs held at the graveside, and Grundy's Sunday was his interment.

clue.text: Succeeds, as the middle 7is destined to

definitions.meaning: of seven days the middle is Thursday, and in the rhyme 'Thursday's child has far to go'

explanation.surface: Someone thrives, as the central one of seven was always going to.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed '7is' is '7 is'. The middle of seven weekdays (Monday to Sunday) is Thursday, and Thursday's child has far to go.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve much success is to travel a long way in life, as the rhyme's Thursday child must.

clue.text: Fixed, with thread in all directions

parts.note: the four compass points south, east, west and north cover every direction
the four compass points south, east, west and north cover every direction
the four compass points south, east, west and north cover every direction
the four compass points south, east, west and north cover every direction

explanation.surface: Something is secured by thread running every which way.
explanation.walkthrough: The four compass points are S, E, W and N, arranged here to make a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Stitched with needle and thread, fastened by stitching.

clue.text: Offer lion, after change of heart, choice piece of meat

parts.note: to tender is to offer, as in tendering a bid

indicators.note: the middle letters, the heart, of the next word are switched around

explanation.surface: Someone offers a lion a prime cut of meat after having second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'heart' of a word is its middle, so a 'change of heart' alters only the inner pair; the big cat becomes a cut of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: The tenderest cut of beef or pork, taken from the loin, is a prized steak.

clue.text: Left mother supporting the girl

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece that supports another sits beneath it

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A mother leaves, leaving the girl to take care of her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb (the mother departed) but is just the abbreviation; in a down answer 'supporting' means sitting underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, as of the heroine of the film Thelma and Louise.

clue.text: Babe, on Friday, is so affectionate (as well as generous)

definitions.text: Babe, on Friday, is so affectionate (as well as generous)

parts.words: Babe, on Friday, is so affectionate (as well as generous)
parts.note: the rhyme says Friday's child is warm-hearted and giving, and the word wanted is the first of that pair

explanation.surface: A baby born at the end of the working week is kind and generous.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme's line is 'Friday's child is loving and giving'; the bracket points to the second quality to steer the solver to the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means tender and devoted, describing an affectionate child.

clue.text: Get intelligence about centre, lines held by retreating enemy

parts.note: the heart is the centre of something

indicators.note: held by says one piece is gripped inside the other
retreating means going backwards, so the word for enemy is turned round

parts.note: a foe is an enemy
L stands for line, so LL is lines

explanation.surface: A spy picks up information about the centre, lines held by a withdrawing army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreating' turns the enemy backwards to EOF, and 'held by' puts the two lines inside to make ELLOF; 'intelligence' is information, as in military intelligence.
explanation.definitionFit: To learn of something by report, to come to know about it through others.

clue.text: Piece of wood, including new pine

indicators.note: including says one piece holds another within it

parts.note: a log is a piece of wood

explanation.surface: A piece of timber contains some fresh pine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like the tree, matching the wood, but it is the verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine is to yearn or ache for something, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Perspective of partners on sex, classically

indicators.note: in an across answer a piece on another follows it

parts.note: sex is Latin for six, written VI in Roman numerals
East and West are partners at bridge

explanation.surface: A classical writer gives a view on relationships and sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sex' is the Latin for six, hence 'classically'; in bridge North-South and East-West play as partners.
explanation.definitionFit: A view is an outlook or point of view, a way of seeing things.

clue.text: Predecessor of 5 Across, married soon after — to a prude?

definitions.text: Predecessor of 5 Across, married soon after — to a prude?

parts.words: Predecessor of 5 Across, married soon after — to a prude?
parts.note: a nursery rhyme figure born on the day before the second weekday and wed on the day after, whose surname is shared with a famously prim Mrs in an old play

explanation.surface: Someone earlier in line wed quickly, perhaps to a prim partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme goes 'born on Monday, christened on Tuesday, married on Wednesday'. Mrs Grundy, from an 18th-century play, stands for prudish disapproval.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's hero was born Monday, before the Tuesday child, and married Wednesday, and shares a surname with Mrs Grundy, symbol of prudery.
